characters: Kofi: a thoughtful fourteen-year-old Ghanaian boy in JHS 3 in the fictional town of Asasekro, wearing a neat cream-and-brown school uniform and carrying a reporter’s notebook for the school civic club.
Ama: Kofi’s fourteen-year-old classmate and co-editor of the school civic club, wearing a cream-and-brown school uniform, natural braided hair with brown clips, and spectacles.
Mrs Mensah: their JHS Social Studies teacher and civic-club patron, wearing a calm teal dress and glasses.
Uncle Yaw: Kofi’s older cousin in his twenties, a young carpenter voting for the first time, wearing a grey work shirt.

narrationPlan.voice: Clear, balanced, non-partisan Ghanaian narrator (en-GH); curious and thoughtful for Kofi and Ama, warm and authoritative for Mrs Mensah.
narrationPlan.pace: Medium (about 125 words per minute); pause clearly on the budget comparisons on pages 6–8.
notes: Pronounce Kofi ("KOH-fee"), Ama ("AH-mah") and Yaw ("YAHW") naturally.

music: Optional subtle acoustic guitar and soft shaker rhythm; off by default.
culturalNotes: Reflects Ghana’s tradition of community town-hall forums and District Assembly participatory budgeting while remaining 100% fictional and non-partisan.
reviewQuestions: Is the story completely free of partisan cues while teaching rigorous budget and civic literacy for JHS 2–3?

pages.brief: Sunny afternoon in a fictional Ghanaian town: Kofi (14, cream-and-brown JHS uniform, notebook) and Ama (14, spectacles, braided hair, cream-and-brown uniform) looking thoughtfully at a worn wooden footbridge over a stream and a small clinic building in the background (no text or banners).
pages.narration: Grounded, observant opening setting up the real community needs in Asasekro.

pages.brief: Lively town square gathering in Ghana (no real party colours, logos, or text banners; neutral purple-and-silver bunting): a speaker in a white tunic gesturing grandly with a microphone while helpers hand small gift boxes to bystanders; Kofi, Ama and cousin Yaw watching from the shade.
pages.narration: Energetic rally scene. Keep Candidate A completely fictional and non-partisan.

pages.brief: Shaded community courtyard: a female candidate in a neat olive-green dress standing beside an easel with a simple bar chart and pie chart (no text or numbers), answering questions from elders, traders and Kofi and Ama.
pages.narration: Contrast the quiet, evidence-based town hall with the flashy handout rally.

pages.brief: Family compound veranda: young carpenter Yaw (grey work shirt) holding a small gift packet while Ama and Kofi sit on a wooden bench with their notebooks open.
pages.narration: Friendly, respectful dialogue between Kofi, Ama and their older cousin.

pages.brief: Sunlit JHS classroom: Mrs Mensah (teal dress, glasses) pointing to a chalkboard diagram showing coins flowing into a central public chest and out to a clinic, water tap and bridge icon (no words or numbers).
pages.narration: Clear, non-partisan civic explanation from Mrs Mensah.

pages.brief: School library table: Kofi and Ama looking at a large official budget binder and a calculator, comparing a small stack of five wooden blocks with a towering stack of fifty blocks (no text).
pages.narration: Walk through the budget arithmetic clearly: 500,000 cedis available vs 5,000,000 cedis promised.

pages.brief: Close view of Ama’s notebook showing three neat visual sketches, a clinic roof, a sturdy bridge, and a water tap, fitting comfortably inside a drawn budget box (no text).
pages.narration: Clear, verifiable arithmetic: 120,000 + 80,000 + 100,000 = 300,000 cedis out of the 500,000-cedi budget.

pages.brief: Evening veranda light: Kofi holding a single small coin beside a thick four-year calendar flipbook while Uncle Yaw looks surprised and thoughtful.
pages.narration: Let the math sink in: 50 cedis over 4 years (1,460 days) is less than 4 pesewas a day.

pages.brief: Peaceful community hall forum: townspeople, elders and youth seated orderly as Uncle Yaw stands at a floor microphone asking a polite question to two candidates seated at a table on stage (no text or partisan symbols).
Civic education table at the community hall: Mrs Mensah demonstrating a private three-sided voting screen and a transparent ballot box (no text) while Uncle Yaw and his friends nod.
pages.narration: Emphasise both tolerance for differing views and the protection of the secret ballot.

pages.brief: Sunny morning outside the community clinic where carpenters are installing new roof sheets: Kofi, Ama, Uncle Yaw and elders checking a visual progress chart mounted on a wooden post (no readable text).
pages.narration: Show that democracy is an ongoing partnership of active citizens and accountable institutions.

pages.brief: Warm morning light: Kofi and Ama walking across a sturdy, newly built wooden-and-concrete footbridge over the stream while Uncle Yaw waves his carpenter’s rule from the bank.

teacherGuide.overview: A strictly non-partisan JHS 2–3 civic education story set in the fictional town of Asasekro. Learners practise evaluating public claims using budget arithmetic, understanding why vote-buying harms long-term service delivery, respecting differing political views, and following up on local government accountability after elections.
learningGoals: Evaluate whether a public promise is credible by comparing its estimated cost against an official budget (300,000 cedis vs 5,000,000 cedis on a 500,000-cedi budget).
Explain why vote-buying undermines public accountability over a four-year (1,460-day) term.
Describe how the secret ballot and peaceful civic debate protect democratic rights.
Explain how citizens and honest public officials work together through post-election budget tracking.

beforeReading: Preview the title and cover illustration with learners and ask what real-world problem or question the characters might face.
whileReading: Pause at the embedded comprehension and vocabulary activities to check understanding and discuss the evidence in the text.
afterReading: Community Budget Challenge: Give groups a fictional 500,000-cedi town budget and a menu of 7 costed community projects (clinic roof, boreholes, footbridge, library books, market drains, streetlights, sports pitch). Ask each group to select and justify a balanced plan that does not exceed 500,000 cedis.
Evidence vs Slogan Sort: Read six fictional campaign statements and classify each as "Specific & Costed Evidence" or "Vague Uncosted Slogan".
discussion: Why did Mrs Mensah remind the class that public projects are funded by taxpayers’ money rather than a politician’s personal pocket?
How did comparing the 500,000-cedi District Assembly budget with each candidate’s promises help Uncle Yaw think differently?
Why does Kofi divide a 50-cedi handout across 1,460 days (4 years), and what happens to public services when elections are treated like cash auctions?
How can citizens ask firm accountability questions while still treating public servants and neighbours with respect?

whatWeKnow: In Ghana’s local government system, Metropolitan, Municipal and District Assemblies (MMDAs) prepare composite budgets and Medium-Term Development Plans funded through Internally Generated Funds (IGF), the District Assemblies Common Fund (DACF) and other statutory transfers.
Under Ghanaian electoral law, bribery, treating and undue influence to buy or coerce votes are electoral offences, and the secrecy of the ballot is guaranteed by the 1992 Constitution.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Civic-technology researchers across Africa study how open-budget dashboards and community scorecards improve local project completion rates.

investigation.title: Cost-Per-Day Civic Maths Check
materials: Exercise book, pencil, and a basic calculator.
steps: Write down the length of a four-year local term in days: 4 × 365 = 1,460 days.
Divide a 50-cedi election handout by 1,460 days (50 ÷ 1,460 ≈ 0.034 cedis, or about 3.4 pesewas per day).
Now compare that 3.4 pesewas per day with the value of clean borehole water and a dry clinic roof serving 5,000 residents every day for 1,460 days.

reviewerNotes: Confirm the vowel in the first syllable (oh vs aw).
Confirm vowel quality and whether the final syllable is stressed.
